power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Introduction: Neurocognitive impairment and depression remain common among people with HIV (PWH), and childhood maltreatment (CM) may further increase vulnerability.

In this cohort, we previously reported that PWH exhibited shorter absolute telomere length, lower MRIbased brain-predicted age difference, and greater epigenetic age acceleration (AA) compared to controls, with limited associations with CM severity.
Building on this, the present study examines whether these markers are linked to neurocognitive performance and depressive symptoms, and whether HIV status or CM severity moderates such associations.

In this study of 238 women (122 PWH), biological aging was assessed using absolute telomere length, mitochondrial DNA copy number, MRI-based brain-predicted age difference, and DNA methylation AA measures, including Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, Horvath intrinsic epigenetic, and Hannum intrinsic epigenetic and extrinsic epigenetic AA.
Neurocognitive performance was measured using a standardised assessment battery and global deficit scores (GDS) were derived.
Depressive symptoms were assessed with the Centre for Epidemiologic Studies -Depression Scale.
Linear regression models examined associations with GDS and depressive symptoms, with interaction models evaluating moderation by HIV status and CM severity.
Results: Biological aging markers were not associated with either neurocognitive performance or depressive symptoms.

Though HIV infection in combination with higher mitochondrial DNA copy number and extrinsic epigenetic AA was nominally associated with higher GDS (p = 0.012 and p = 0.047, respectively), these associations did not survive correction for multiple testing.
Neither HIV nor CM moderated the association between biological aging markers and depression scores.

Conclusions: Despite accelerated biological aging being evident in PWH, we found limited evidence of association with neurocognitive performance or depressive symptoms, underscoring their multifactorial nature.
Larger longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these markers predict neurocognitive and psychiatric trajectories.

Neurocognitive impairment and depression are two of the most prevalent and debilitating outcomes affecting people with HIV (PWH). 1, 2 HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) affect approximately 50% of PWH globally. 3 Depression, likewise, affects over 280 million people globally and occurs at rates nearly three times higher in PWH compared to the general population. [4] [5] [6] [7] Both disorders disproportionally affect women, who face unique psychosocial and biological vulnerabilities. [8] [9] [10] Evidence suggests that HIV adversely influences neurocognition and depression through chronic neuroinflammation and direct neurotoxicity. 1, 11, 12 Viral persistence in microglia, astrocytes, and memory T cells sustains immune activation, leading to elevated cytokine release, oxidative stress, and synaptic injury. 11, 13, 14 This inflammatory milieu disrupts neural circuits involved in cognition and mood regulation, thereby increasing risk for HAND and depression. 1, 2 Childhood maltreatment (CM), encompassing physical, sexual, and emotional abuse as well as physical and emotional neglect, further compounds this risk. 12, 15 Mechanistically, CM induces long-lasting dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, leading to altered cortisol secretion, heightened stress reactivity, and downstream structural changes in brain regions such as the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. [16] [17] [18] CM is highly prevalent globally, with particularly elevated rates in sub-Saharan Africa. [19] [20] [21] In South Africa, women are disproportionately affected by both HIV and CM, warranting investigations into how the dual burden of these stressors contributes to neurocognitive and affective outcomes. 19, [22] [23] [24] [25] Emerging evidence suggests that biological aging, the progressive decline in physiological function across molecular, cellular, tissue, and organ systems, may serve as a shared pathway linking HIV, CM, neurocognitive impairment, and depression (Bell et al., 2019; Ferrucci et al.,   2020).

text.text: Exploring this intersection can help determine whether dual exposure amplifies vulnerability to neurocognitive and psychiatric outcomes, or whether each factor contributes through independent mechanisms.

This study therefore aims to examine associations between multiple biological aging markers, including absolute TL (aTL), mtDNAcn, MRI-BPAD, and DNAmAge clocks, and two outcomes assessed separately: global deficit scores (GDS) and depressive symptom scores.

Given evidence linking HIV and CM to accelerated biological aging and neuropsychiatric vulnerability, we further hypothesised that HIV status and CM severity would modify the associations between biological aging and GDS and depressive symptoms, such that these associations would be stronger among PWH with greater CM severity.
This cross-sectional analysis drew on baseline data from 238 women enrolled between 2008 and 2015 in a longitudinal study in Cape Town, South Africa (122 PWH).
The study received ethics approval from the Health Research Ethics Committee (HREC) of Stellenbosch University, Cape Town, South Africa, and is renewed annually (project ethics code: N07/07/153).
All participants provided informed consent, and the study was conducted in accordance with the recommendations of the Declaration of Helsinki.
Participants were recruited from community health care facilities and completed sociodemographic and neuropsychological assessments, along with blood collection.

Due to data availability, biological aging measures were available for subsets of the cohort i.e., aTL and mtDNAcn for 210 women (105 PWH), MRI-BPAD for 202 (105 PWH), and DNAmAge clocks for 231 (120 PWH).

Recruitment procedures have been described previously. 40 Eligible participants were aged 18-50 years, literate in English/Afrikaans/isiXhosa, medically stable, and psychotropic medication-naïve (including antidepressants).

text.text: Exclusion criteria included major psychiatric illness, substance use disorder, significant medical comorbidities, prior head injury with over 24 hours loss of consciousness, probable dementia, opportunistic central nervous system (CNS) infection or neoplasm, hepatitis B, or MRI contraindications.
HIV infection was determined by enzyme linked immunosorbent assay.

For PWH, immunovirological markers were assessed, including CD4+ T cell count (indicator of immune function and disease progression) and CD8+ T cell count (reflecting immune activation), CD4:CD8 ratio (marker of immune balance), and plasma viral load (measure of treatment response and ongoing viral replication).

Neurocognitive performance was assessed using the HIV Neurobehavioral Research Center (HNRC) neuropsychological test 41 , comprising 17 tests across seven domains sensitive to HIV effects: attention/working memory, learning, delayed recall, executive function, motor ability, information processing speed, and verbal fluency. 42 Raw scores were adjusted using locally derived normative prediction equations based on a sample of 500 South African adults without HIV (Deist et al., 2023).

text.text: Whole-blood DNA concentration and purity were evaluated using a Qubit 4 fluorometer (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA) or NanoDrop One spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA).
Samples were normalised to 350 ng of total DNA and diluted to 6 ng/µL prior to methylation profiling.
DNA methylation profiling was performed at the University of Minnesota Genomics Center using the Infinium MethylationEPIC v2 BeadChip (Illumina, San Diego, CA).

Quality control and preprocessing were conducted in R using the ENmix pipeline 49 , including assessment and exclusion of low-quality probes and samples based on detection P values, bead counts, bisulfite-conversion intensity, and outlier detection.

text.text: Age acceleration was defined as the difference between estimated DNAmAge and chronological age.

Cellular aging was indexed through aTL and mtDNAcn, which were measured simultaneously in triplicate using the absolute human TL and mtDNAcn dual quantification quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assay kit (ScienCell Research Laboratories, Carlsbad, CA; Catalog number 8958) on a QuantStudio 6 Pro Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
Samples were analysed in triplicate according to the manufacturer's protocols.
Absolute TL was expressed as kilobases per chromosome end, and mtDNAcn was expressed as mitochondrial DNA copies per diploid cell.

T1-weighted MRI-based brain-predicted age (MRI-BPA) was assessed using the brainageR pipeline. 32 This model applies Gaussian process regression to voxel-wise tissue maps derived from SPM12 preprocessing and was trained on 3377 healthy adults aged 18 -92 years and has been validated across multiple cohorts. All models were adjusted for age, age-squared (to account for the non-linear association between MRI-BPA and chronological age 56 ), MRI protocol type (MRI-BPAD models), plate number (aTL and mtDNAcn models), and LEC scores (CTQ-SF analyses).

text.text: The present study examined whether multiple measures of biological aging, including aTL, mtDNAcn, MRI-BPAD, and DNAmAge clocks (HorvathAA, HannumAA, PhenoAA, Horvath IEAA, Hannum IEAA, and EEAA), were associated with overall neurocognitive performance and depressive symptoms, and whether these relationships were moderated by HIV status and CM severity.
PWH had shorter aTL, lower MRI-BPAD, greater HorvathAA, HannumAA, PhenoAA, and EEAA than controls.
CM was not linked to biological aging markers.
Across all models, none of the biological aging markers were significantly associated with neurocognitive performance or depressive symptom severity.
Furthermore, there was little evidence that HIV status or CM consistently modified these associations.

The limited relationships between biological aging markers and neurocognitive performance or depressive symptoms suggest that these outcomes are likely influenced by multiple interacting mechanisms, including neuroinflammation, vascular dysfunction, metabolic alterations, psychosocial stress, and neurodegeneration, of which biological aging represents only one component. [58] [59] [60] It is also plausible that accelerated biological aging precedes clinically detectable neuropsychiatric changes, with poor neurocognitive performance or depressive symptoms emerging only after prolonged cumulative biological burden. 61, 62 Longitudinal studies will be critical to determine whether accelerated biological aging predicts decline or symptom onset over time in vulnerable populations.

text.text: Our findings differ from several studies reporting associations between accelerated biological aging and poorer global neurocognitive impairment 63, 64 or greater depressive symptom severity 65 , particularly among PWH.

text.text: However, evidence across the field remains mixed, with some studies reporting null or weak associations with neurocognitive impairment 66, 67 or depression 68, 69 .

text.text: Methodological and cohort differences may partly explain these discrepancies.

Prior studies were conducted predominately in high-income countries and mixed-sex cohorts 32, 63, 65 , whereas our cohort comprised South African women, a population disproportionately affected by both HIV and CM 19, 23, 24 .

text.text: Our study cohort was also relatively young, and biological aging effects may be more pronounced in older populations.

Sex differences in biological aging and neuropsychiatric vulnerability have been reported 70, 71 , raising the possibility that associations between biological aging and neuropsychiatric outcomes vary across populations and contexts.

text.text: Measurement considerations may also contribute.
While the GDS is a well validated global measure of neurocognitive performance 64, 72, 73 , it may be less sensitive to subtle domain-specific associations that have been reported in PWH 74, 75 .

text.text: Telomere dynamics may reflect both attrition and compensatory elongation processes, complicating interpretation in cross sectional designs. 85, 86 Similarly, mtDNAcn measured in peripheral blood may not accurately capture mitochondrial function within the CNS, and estimates can be confounded by platelet leukocyte ratios or technical variability in qPCR assays. [87] [88] [89] These considerations underscore the importance of evaluating biological aging across diverse populations, employing both global and domain specific neurocognitive measures, validated depression instruments, and multimodal brain imaging to capture region specific vulnerability.

text.text: We found little evidence that HIV status or CM consistently modified the relationships between biological aging markers and neurocognitive performance or depressive symptoms.

Although several nominal interactions involving mtDNAcn and EEAA were observed, none remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons, underscoring the limited evidence of robust moderation effects in this cohort.
To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine interactions between biological aging markers, HIV, and CM in relation to neurocognitive performance and depressive symptoms.
Replication in larger longitudinal cohorts will be important to determine whether subtle interaction effects emerge over time.

While moderation effects were not observed, PWH demonstrated accelerated biological aging across several markers, including shorter aTL and greater epigenetic age acceleration, whereas MRI-BPAD was lower compared to controls.

These results, reported in detail elsewhere 57 , are consistent with prior evidence linking HIV to telomere shortening and epigenetic age acceleration. 29, 30, 32, 67 Together, they support the idea that persistent immune activation, neuronal injury, and cellular senescence contribute to accelerated biological aging in HIV. 29, 30 In contrast, CM severity showed little evidence of association with biological aging markers in this cohort, echoing the mixed findings across prior studies. 27, [90] [91] [92] These contextual results provide background for interpreting the limited moderation effects observed here and emphasise the importance of future work disentangling shared versus distinct pathways through which HIV and CM may influence biological aging.

text.text: This study has several limitations worth noting.

The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the relatively small sample size yielded wide confidence intervals, limiting the precision of our estimates of interaction effects. 93 CM was assessed retrospectively and is therefore susceptible to recall bias. 94 Neuroimaging analyses were limited to a single modality, and additional modalities such as functional MRI or diffusion tensor imaging may provide more sensitive markers of brain aging. 95, 96 Finally, the high amplification efficiency observed in the mtDNAcn qPCR serial dilution indicates the results should be interpreted cautiously due to potential technical variability. 57 Despite these limitations, the present study has several strengths, including the use of normative neurocognitive performance scores to reduce sociodemographic bias 44, 45 , validation of the brainageR model in a South African cohort, measurement of aTL rather than relative TL to provide a more direct index of telomere dynamics 85 , and a multimarker approach spanning molecular, cellular, and structural domains of biological aging.

text.text: Accelerated biological aging was evident among PWH but was not associated with neurocognitive performance or depressive symptoms, suggesting that these biological changes alone may be insufficient to explain cognitive and depressive symptomatology.
Instead, accelerated biological aging may represent a marker of vulnerability within a broader multifactorial disease process.

Larger longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these markers predict neurocognitive performance or depressive symptoms over time, and whether these trajectories are modified by HIV infection and CM.
